blocks.content: Japanese uses three writing systems simultaneously, and most sentences mix all three. Understanding *why* each script exists makes the whole system feel less overwhelming.

**Hiragana** (ひらがな) is the backbone of the written language — 46 base characters, each representing one syllable. It covers native Japanese words, grammatical particles, verb endings, and anything with no kanji equivalent. If you know no kanji, you can write everything in hiragana and be understood.

**Katakana** (カタカナ) represents the exact same sounds as hiragana but is visually distinct — angular where hiragana is rounded. It marks foreign loanwords, borrowed proper nouns, scientific terms, and onomatopoeia. Seeing katakana is a reliable signal: this word came from somewhere else.

**Kanji** (漢字) are Chinese-origin characters that carry meaning directly. A single kanji can pack the meaning of a whole English word into one character. The 常用漢字 standard defines 2,136 characters used in everyday writing; fluent readers know several thousand.
A Real Sentence

rows.japanese: 私はコーヒーが好きです。
rows.romaji: Watashi wa koohii ga suki desu.

blocks.content: Reading a Japanese sentence is not harder once you accept that the script-switching is carrying information. Katakana = likely foreign word. Kanji = meaning anchor. Hiragana = grammatical glue.

Japanese is a **Subject–Object–Verb** language — the verb always comes last. This is the single biggest structural difference from English, and it affects everything: you have to hold the subject and object in your head before the action resolves at the end of the sentence.

rows.japanese: 私はコーヒーを飲みます。
彼はかばんを買いました。

rows.english: The dog is chasing the cat.
rows.japanese: 犬が猫を追いかけています。
rows.romaji: Inu ga neko wo oikakete imasu.

blocks.content: Modifiers — adjectives, relative clauses, entire subordinate phrases — also always come *before* the noun they describe, not after. This means long sentences stack up heavily at the beginning and resolve at the end.

In long sentences, native speakers reach the verb at the very end and finally know what happened. This is why listening in Japanese feels like waiting for the punchline. With practice, you start anticipating the verb class early from context.

lessons.title: Topic は vs Subject が

blocks.content: Japanese draws a distinction that English collapses into one slot. **は** marks the *topic* — what the sentence is *about*. **が** marks the *subject* — who or what *performs* or *experiences* the predicate.

rows.romaji: Neko wa sakana ga suki desu.
rows.note: 猫は = topic; 魚が = subject of 好き

rows.romaji: Watashi wa atama ga itai desu.
rows.note: 私は = topic; 頭が = subject of 痛い
象は = topic; 鼻が = subject of 長い

blocks.content: は often translates as "as for ~" or "speaking of ~" — it sets the frame for everything that follows. が identifies *who* is doing or experiencing something. Many beginners use が everywhere at first; は is how you signal that you are talking *about* something, not just naming it.

Common mistake: using が when は is correct makes sentences sound like new information or contrast is being introduced. 私**が**田中です would mean "It is *I* who is Tanaka" — implying there was a question about which person. 私**は**田中です is simply "I am Tanaka."

In English, modifiers can appear on either side of a noun. In Japanese, they always come *before* the noun they describe — adjectives, relative clauses, and entire subordinate phrases all stack up before their noun.

rows.japanese: 田中さんが作ったケーキ

blocks.content: Relative clauses in Japanese require no relative pronoun — no "that", "which", or "who". You simply place the entire clause before the noun: 昨日読んだ stacks directly onto any following noun.

Japanese regularly omits the subject when it is clear from context. This is called *pro-drop*, and it is the rule rather than the exception in natural speech. Writing or saying わかりました is not incomplete — the subject is understood.

What looks like ambiguity is resolved by context. Once "I" or "she" has been established as the topic, Japanese speakers do not keep repeating it. If you cannot tell who the subject is in a real conversation, that is normal — context does the work.

Japanese has no spaces between words. Word boundaries are legible because the three scripts alternate predictably, and because readers have internalised the grammar. The punctuation system is its own, parallel to the Western one.
Punctuation Marks

rows.name: Touten
rows.use: Comma — marks a pause within a sentence

rows.name: Nijū kagikakko
rows.use: Nested quotation marks, or book and work titles

rows.name: Nakaguro
rows.use: Separates list items or parts of a foreign name

rows.name: Chōonpu
rows.use: Extends a vowel sound in katakana words

rows.name: Full-width forms
rows.use: Same function as English, but full-width for alignment

blocks.content: In Japanese fiction and manga, 「」kagikakko are the standard dialogue markers — not Western-style quotation marks. You will encounter them constantly in native texts.
Examples in Context

rows.japanese: 私はりんご、みかん、ぶどうを買いました。
rows.romaji: Watashi wa ringo, mikan, budō wo kaimashita.
rows.english: I bought apples, oranges, and grapes.

blocks.content: Writing Direction

Modern Japanese is written horizontally, left to right. Traditional texts — novels, some newspapers, manga speech bubbles — run *vertically* in columns read right to left. Both directions are in active use today.
A small っ signals a short, sharp pause before the following consonant, which is then held slightly longer. It occupies one full mora — one beat of rhythm — like any other kana.

lines: → the pause doubles the following consonant

blocks.content: Common mistake: without the っ, the meaning changes entirely. きて (*kite*) = "come!" — completely different from きって (*kitte*, postage stamp). Treat っ as a real beat of silence, not an ornament.
Small や, ゆ, よ combine with a preceding consonant + i kana to form a single blended syllable. The i vowel disappears and the two characters collapse into one sound.

lines: [consonant + i kana] + **ゃ / ゅ / ょ** → one syllable, not two

rows.one syllable: 4 mora: びょ・う・い・ん

blocks.content: びょういん (hospital) and びよういん (beauty salon) are frequently confused — the first has a small よ (one syllable), the second has a full-size よ (two syllables). The written distinction is crucial.
Holding a vowel for one extra mora changes meaning. Vowel length is phonemically significant in Japanese — two otherwise identical words can differ only in how long a vowel is held.
How Long Vowels Are Written

lines: Hiragana: repeat the vowel (or **お + う** for the ō sound)

blocks.content: The ー mark only appears in katakana. In hiragana words, the long vowel is spelled out explicitly (ああ, おう, etc.). The difference between おじさん and おじいさん is one extra い — easy to miss in handwriting.

English stress makes one syllable *louder*. Japanese **pitch accent** makes one syllable *higher* in tone. Every word has a pitch pattern, and in some cases the pattern is the only thing distinguishing two otherwise identical words.
The Tokyo dialect (standard Japanese) is the reference system used in textbooks and broadcast media. Pitch is described as H (high) or L (low) per mora.
High and Low Patterns
橋 and 箸 look identical in romaji and share the same kanji sounds — pitch is the *only* distinguishing feature. In a real sentence, context almost always resolves meaning before pitch even matters.
For Learners

Getting pitch accent wrong does not prevent communication. Native speakers adjust easily for non-native speech. Pitch is best absorbed through listening — it improves naturally with exposure and can be studied deliberately at intermediate level. For now, focus on vocabulary, grammar, and reading.
